https://slguardian.org/ceuta-crisis-spar.text: Ceuta migration crisis The recent migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta has prompted renewed discussion over the European Union’s approach to border management, migration, and humanitarian responsibility. While governments have concentrated on security measures and immediate policy responses, the events have also inspired broader reflections on Europe’s identity and its treatment of migrants. In an opinion essay published by the German weekly Die Zeit , the crisis is examined through the lens of Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey , with the newspaper using the film to explore the tensions between security, hospitality, and the moral responsibilities of modern societies. According to Die Zeit , Nolan’s adaptation places these themes at the centre of its narrative from the opening scenes. The newspaper notes that the film introduces “people from the sea”, figures who are portrayed as a source of anxiety for Ithaca’s ruling class, which fears an invasion threatening what it regards as the pinnacle of Greek civilisation. At the same time, Die Zeit highlights the film’s emphasis on Zeus’ law of hospitality, known as Xenia, under which strangers are to be welcomed and offered food and shelter because any traveller, regardless of appearance or wealth, could be a disguised god. The newspaper argues that this contrast between fear and hospitality provides a striking parallel with present-day Europe. According to Die Zeit , while the fictional society of Ithaca oscillates between military defence and welcoming strangers, contemporary Europe increasingly applies different standards to different categories of migrants. Rather than simply opening or closing borders, the newspaper contends that European migration policy has evolved into a system of selective access. To develop this argument, Die Zeit draws on the work of sociologist Steffen Mau and his 2021 description of borders as “sorting machines”. The newspaper argues that borders now function as mechanisms that determine who may enter and who must remain outside. It notes that affluent tourists, privileged expatriates, highly sought-after skilled workers, and seasonal labourers needed to address labour shortages continue to enjoy mobility, while those who do not fit these categories face increasingly restrictive barriers. As an example, Die Zeit refers to Germany’s so-called “asparagus airlift” in 2020, when thousands of Romanian agricultural workers were flown into Germany despite COVID-19 lockdown restrictions. The newspaper contrasts that episode with the recent events in Ceuta, where approximately 50,000 migrants—many described as young Moroccans—attempted to enter the Spanish enclave after reportedly being influenced by false information circulating on social media suggesting they could continue onwards to mainland Spain. The opinion essay also examines the political reaction within Europe. According to Die Zeit , Spain received little visible solidarity from fellow European Union member states during the crisis. The newspaper further notes that 22 EU heads of government, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, signed an open letter attributing at least part of the responsibility for the crisis to Spain’s highest court. That court had recently ruled that migrants reaching Ceuta and Melilla by sea should not be subjected to immediate pushbacks but instead should be given access to asylum procedures. Using Steffen Mau’s concepts of “opening globalisation” and “closing globalisation”, Die Zeit argues that the European Union’s internal freedom of movement is closely connected to the fortification of its external borders. According to the newspaper, the ability of people to move freely within the Schengen Area depends upon stronger controls at Europe’s external frontiers, creating a system in which internal mobility and external restrictions reinforce one another. Beyond border policy, Die Zeit argues that efforts to combat irregular migration have become one of the defining political priorities for governments across Europe. The newspaper observes that even critics of the existing border regime rarely advocate a comprehensive alternative. In support of this argument, it cites British historian Perry Anderson, who reportedly argued in April 2025 that Europe’s political left struggles to present a politically consistent and coherent position on migration, limiting its ability to challenge conservative approaches. The newspaper identifies Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as an illustration of this broader political reality. According to Die Zeit , Sánchez has continued strengthening Spain’s external borders while cooperating closely with Morocco and Algeria on migration policy. Following the events in Ceuta, he travelled to the enclave to make clear that Moroccan migrants should not expect onward travel to mainland Spain. At the same time, Spanish authorities were reported to be installing additional barriers in the water to reduce the likelihood of similar crossings. The newspaper also notes that most migrants had already returned to Morocco, partly because they found neither food nor drinking water after reaching Ceuta. While Die Zeit acknowledges what it describes as a broad European political consensus in favour of stricter border controls, it argues that the official response to the deaths recorded during the crisis deserves closer examination. Referring to official reports identifying 72 fatalities, with police expecting additional bodies to be recovered, the newspaper observes that these deaths were not mentioned in the open letter signed by European leaders. It also notes that when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen referred to the “unacceptable images” from Ceuta, her remarks did not explicitly refer to those who had drowned. To interpret this response, Die Zeit invokes the work of the late sociologist Zygmunt Bauman and his concept of the “adiaphorisation of migration”. According to the newspaper, Bauman used the term to describe situations in which migrants cease to be viewed primarily through moral considerations. Die Zeit argues that this concept provides a framework for understanding why, in its view, those who died during the Ceuta crisis received relatively little public acknowledgement in official political discourse. The newspaper further compares European communication surrounding migration with that of the administration of former US President Donald Trump. According to Die Zeit , while the Trump administration openly projected a hard-line approach to immigration through public messaging and social media, European governments have generally responded with greater restraint when fatalities occur at external borders such as Ceuta, Lesbos, and Lampedusa. The newspaper argues that the principal distinction lies in political communication rather than necessarily in the underlying objective of border control, presenting this as its interpretation of current migration policy. In its concluding reflections, Die Zeit returns to Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey and draws upon interpretations of Odysseus presented by philosophers Theodor W. Adorno and Max Horkheimer in Dialectic of Enlightenment . The newspaper notes that Nolan’s film ultimately depicts Odysseus acknowledging that he and his companions themselves have become the feared “people from the sea”. According to Die Zeit , this ending suggests that the capacity for brutality exists not only beyond the borders of civilisation but also within it. Framed as an opinion essay rather than a news report, the article uses the events in Ceuta to encourage reflection on how Europe reconciles border security, humanitarian responsibility, and the values it seeks to uphold in an increasingly polarised migration debate. https://www.wbaa.org/npr-news/2026-08-12.text: On Air Now Playing WBAA News 101.3 FM and AM 920 On Air Now Playing WBAA Jazz 101.3 FM HD3 On Air Now Playing WBAA Classical 105.9 FM & HD-2 NPR White House press secretary leaving NPR | By Deepa Shivaram Published August 12, 2026 at 4:05 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 2:35 SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on July 23, 2026. Updated August 13, 2026 at 8:23 AM EDT White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is leaving her role at the end of the month to spend more time with family, President Trump said Wednesday. She will continue to be an outside adviser, he added. "Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect!," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Leavitt, 28, was the youngest ever White House press secretary. She recently returned from parental leave after the birth of her second child in May. "The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she said on social media . Leavitt's departure comes as the president, and his party, are struggling with voters who disapprove of his handling of the economy and high prices amid the Iran war. In his post, Trump said Leavitt would still be an "influential voice" for the GOP. Leavitt first started working for Trump in his first administration in 2020 and left shortly before his term ended. She later made an unsuccessful run for Congress in her home state of New Hampshire. Later, she went on to work for Trump's super PAC before working for Trump's 2024 campaign. It's not yet clear who will replace her; several Cabinet secretaries filled in for Leavitt while she was on parental leave. At the podium, Leavitt was often confrontational with the press corps, criticizing some outlets for what she described as bias. She was a staunch defender of Trump's policies even on issues such as denying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump continues to falsely say he won. The start of her tenure also came with mounting tensions with the press corps. After The Associated Press refused to call the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America," their reporters lost access to White House events and inclusion in travel with the president as part of the traveling press corps. New media outlets, many with coverage that supports the president's agenda, were included in the briefing room and on Air Force One. Press access to Leavitt and other senior communication officials were also cut last October. Journalists used to be able to walk into the area called "upper press" but now an appointment is required. Trump would often compliment Leavitt at events at the White House, calling her a "superstar." During a meeting at the White House with Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in November, Trump joked that the prime minister wanted Leavitt to work for him in Hungary. "That's a very good decision you just made," Trump said to Orbán, before turning to Leavitt. "Please don't leave us, Karoline." Skip next section Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday. It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation . The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said. The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported. The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities. "For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw . For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said. The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported. What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children? The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms. "Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying. The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children. It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said. Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year. France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move . The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia. "As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio. The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country. The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil." "These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said. The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials. The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan. He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat. Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video https://p.dw.com/p/5OLtx Skip next section Student leader Neha Bora released from detention 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Student leader Neha Bora released from detention Bora was also detained in early October Image: ANI/IMAGO All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during the latest protest in New Delhi on Friday was released later in the night. Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's top poll official. Speaking to the media after her release, Bora called for Dipke and other protesters to be released, saying that they had been "illegally detained". "They are ordinary citizens demanding accountability and their right to vote. Carrying out such illegal detentions and keeping people at the police station overnight makes no sense at all," Bora said. A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year. Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is being questioned. The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy". BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday. Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder." "It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said. https://p.dw.com/p/5OLr3 Skip next section CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports The 'Cockroach' movement has called Dipke's detention a 'kidnapping' Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said. Dipke was arrested to ‌prevent a ⁠breach ⁠of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported. CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC). Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him. The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping." "Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts. Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place. Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car. Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke. Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest. The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area. "The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X. Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations. The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign. The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said. Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists. They were released after nearly 24 hours. The world's largest democracy has seen almost daily protests since the start of October. The youth-led ' Cockroach ' movement, opposition parties, student organizations and civil society members are calling for India's election chief to step down over a sweeping revision of voter rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). On Friday, another protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at a key business district in the heart of Delhi culminated in detentions. CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken away in a police car even before he could get to the protest location. It was the second time that Dipke was detained in less than a week . Reports now say that the 'Cockroach' founder has been arrested following his detention, and is due to appear before a Special Executive Magistrate court today. With protests being prohibited and demonstrations ending in detentions, the stir over accountability and electoral reform has also sparked a debate over the public's right to protest. Meanwhile, a group of Democratic lawmakers in the US have called on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India next week, to raise with Indian officials the alleged wrongful detentions and excessive use of force during the student protests in New Delhi and other parts of the country.
